disease_name_scope: Pure disease leaf name only. Drug exposure, infection trigger, BSA, SCORTEN, and culprit attribution are represented as axes, risk/context factors, or treatment modifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Presentation of drug, drug-metabolite, or infection-associated antigen to susceptible T cells. This is the upstream sensitization and elicitation mechanism, but the specific trigger remains context rather than part of the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cytotoxic CD8 T-cell and NK-cell activation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Expansion and tissue trafficking of cytotoxic lymphocytes producing granulysin, perforin, granzyme B, Fas ligand, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma. This is the proximate immune effector mechanism for epidermal necrolysis.

Diffuse keratinocyte death with full-thickness epidermal necrosis and dermo-epidermal separation. The intensity of this mechanism maps to dusky targetoid macules, flaccid bullae, Nikolsky sign, and detached BSA.
The same cytotoxic epithelial injury affects oral, ocular, genital, gastrointestinal, and airway mucosa, causing erosions, pain, poor oral intake, diarrhea, ocular surface loss, and airway risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Skin barrier failure with fluid, heat, and protein loss
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Denuded skin behaves physiologically like a partial-thickness burn: evaporative heat loss, fluid loss, electrolyte derangement, hypoalbuminemia, pain, and vulnerability to shock and acute kidney injury.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic inflammatory and catabolic stress response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Fever, CRP elevation, tachycardia, cytopenias or leukocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, and hepatic stress arising from epithelial necrolysis, cytokines, pain, and secondary infection pressure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Secondary wound infection and sepsis pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Loss of epidermal and mucosal barriers enables wound colonization, bacteremia, candidemia, pneumonia, urinary infection, and septic shock. This is a frequent downstream complication rather than the disease identity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Ocular surface epithelial sloughing and inflammation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Conjunctival and corneal epithelial injury causes pain, photophobia, epithelial defects, pseudomembranes, symblepharon, dry eye, corneal scarring, and long-term visual loss.

Less common but high-impact epithelial injury involving tracheobronchial and gastrointestinal surfaces, causing hypoxemia, airway obstruction, pneumonia risk, diarrhea, bleeding, and nutritional failure.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Antigen presentation in susceptible hosts expands cytotoxic effector cells.
Granulysin, perforin/granzyme, Fas-FasL, and TNF-alpha signaling kill keratinocytes and produce full-thickness epidermal necrosis.
The immune injury is directed against epithelial surfaces, so mucosal erosions commonly accompany skin necrolysis.
Early epidermal injury appears as dusky erythematous macules and atypical targetoid lesions.
Dermo-epidermal cleavage produces flaccid bullae before sheet-like detachment.
Epidermal instability causes skin to shear with tangential pressure.
Detached BSA is the direct clinical surface measure of epidermal necrolysis severity.
Denuded dermis and active epithelial necrosis cause severe skin pain and burning.
Multisite mucosal erosions are part of the same epithelial necrolysis process.
Oral erosions, hemorrhagic crusting, odynophagia, and poor intake are common.
Genital erosions and later adhesions are common and clinically important.
Conjunctival and corneal epithelial defects measure acute ocular involvement.
Acute ocular epithelial injury can transition to symblepharon, dry eye, corneal scarring, and visual loss.
Large denuded BSA produces evaporative and exudative loss that can cause hypovolemia and shock.
Hypovolemia, sepsis, nephrotoxic exposures, and baseline renal disease increase AKI risk.
Protein loss through denuded skin plus inflammation lowers albumin.
Fever is common in the prodrome and acute phase.
Pain, fever, hypovolemia, and systemic stress commonly cause tachycardia; heart rate is a SCORTEN component.
Inflammation and secondary infection pressure elevate CRP.
Leukocytosis, leukopenia, neutrophilia, and lymphopenia can all occur depending on severity, trigger, marrow reserve, infection, and medications.
Severe systemic illness, marrow suppression, infection, DIC, or transplant/drug context can lower platelets.
Skin and mucosal barrier loss increases wound infection and line/pulmonary/urinary infection risk.
Secondary infection can progress to bacteremia or septic shock.
Airway epithelial sloughing, aspiration, pneumonia, and ARDS may require intubation.
Gastrointestinal mucosal sloughing can cause diarrhea, bleeding, feeding intolerance, and translocation risk.
Respiratory failure is a major short-term mortality pathway.
Sepsis and septic shock are leading causes of death in epidermal necrolysis.
AKI reflects shock, renal reserve, and organ failure; BUN is a SCORTEN component.
Shock from barrier failure, fever, pain, and poor intake increases early mortality.

axes.shape_free_text: Dusky erythematous macules, atypical target lesions, or purpuric macules before or during epidermal detachment.
Flaccid bullae and coalescing blisters caused by dermo-epidermal separation.
Epidermal shearing or detachment after tangential pressure.
Percent total body surface area with detached or detachable epidermis. SJS <10%, overlap 10-30%, TEN >30%, but the disease leaf covers the full SJS/TEN spectrum.
Percent BSA with erythematous, dusky, purpuric, blistering, eroded, or detached mucocutaneous eruption, including non-detached involved skin.
Integrated severity of denuded skin, exudation, heat loss, wound pain, dressing burden, and infection entry risk.
Burning skin pain, tenderness, odynophagia-related pain, or painful denuded dermis.
Any mucosal erosions or sloughing across oral, ocular, genital, gastrointestinal, or airway surfaces.
Oral erosions, hemorrhagic lip crusting, odynophagia, and inability to eat or drink from oral mucosal injury.
Conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, epithelial defects, corneal sloughing, pseudomembranes, or eyelid-margin ulceration in acute SJS/TEN.
Genital erosions, ulceration, crusting, dysuria from mucosal injury, or early adhesion risk.
Diarrhea, GI bleeding, feeding intolerance, esophageal sloughing, or other gastrointestinal epithelial injury attributable to SJS/TEN.
Airway epithelial sloughing, bronchoscopy evidence, stridor, airway bleeding, or respiratory decline from epithelial necrolysis.
Fever is common in the prodrome and acute phase; hypothermia may indicate late shock or frailty.
Tachycardia reflects fever, pain, hypovolemia, sepsis, anemia, or SCORTEN risk.
Hypotension reflects fluid loss, sepsis, bleeding, or late multiorgan failure.
Reduced oxygen saturation may reflect airway involvement, pneumonia, aspiration, ARDS, or sepsis.
Variable WBC response; leukopenia and lymphopenia can mark severe disease or medication/transplant context, while leukocytosis can mark infection or stress.
Neutrophilia may reflect stress or secondary infection; neutropenia can reflect drug marrow toxicity, transplant context, or severe systemic illness.
Lymphopenia is common in severe acute illness and has been associated with poor SJS/TEN outcomes.
Thrombocytopenia can reflect marrow suppression, infection, DIC, transplant context, or severe systemic inflammation.
Inflammation marker; high values may reflect epidermal necrolysis, secondary infection, or both.
Renal perfusion/reserve marker and SCORTEN component.
Renal reserve and AKI marker; background CKD should adjust fallback separately.
Low bicarbonate is a SCORTEN component and may reflect shock, AKI, diarrhea, or sepsis.
Stress hyperglycemia and diabetes context; glucose >252 mg/dL is a SCORTEN component.
Hyponatremia or hypernatremia from fluid loss, poor intake, renal disease, or critical illness.
Hypoalbuminemia from inflammation, malnutrition, protein loss, and critical illness.
Hepatic or systemic injury marker; can rise from drug injury, shock, infection, or muscle injury context.
Hepatic injury marker; mild to moderate rises are common in severe drug reactions and critical illness.
Probability that a recent medication exposure is the culprit for the current epidermal necrolysis episode. This context is not a disease-name restriction.
Time from suspected culprit start or re-exposure to prodrome or first rash; used for context and causality, not as a disease-name qualifier.
Extent to which suspected culprit and close cross-reactive medications have been stopped.
Probability that infection is an eliciting trigger or competing explanation; kept as context rather than disease-name content.
Prognostic composite score using age, malignancy, detached BSA, heart rate, BUN, bicarbonate, and glucose. Use as severity context when individual components are incomplete.
Healing phase with epithelial regrowth, reduced exudation, and wound stabilization.
Hazard of wound infection, pneumonia, line infection, UTI, or fungal infection after barrier loss or immunomodulatory treatment.
Hazard of secondary infection progressing to sepsis or septic shock during SJS/TEN.
Hazard of hypovolemia, hypotension, and shock from skin/mucosal fluid loss, fever, poor intake, and pain.
AKI hazard from hypovolemia, sepsis, baseline renal disease, nephrotoxic drugs, and critical illness.
Hazard of hypoxemic respiratory failure from airway sloughing, pneumonia, aspiration, sepsis, or ARDS.
ARDS hazard from severe systemic inflammation, pneumonia, aspiration, sepsis, fluid overload, or airway epithelial injury.
Hazard of symblepharon, severe dry eye, corneal scarring, limbal stem cell deficiency, or visual loss after acute ocular SJS/TEN.

Lifespan outcome hazard for Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis. Driven by detached BSA, age, malignancy, renal dysfunction, acidosis, hyperglycemia, shock, sepsis, respiratory failure, and delayed supportive care.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Larger denuded BSA increases fluid and heat loss.
Large open skin surface increases colonization, wound infection, and invasive infection risk.
Severe oral erosions and odynophagia reduce oral intake.
Untreated acute ocular epithelial loss causes symblepharon and corneal scarring.
Airway epithelial injury may cause obstruction, pneumonia, aspiration, or intubation need.
Barrier-related infection can become bacteremia or septic shock.
Detached BSA is a core severity measure and part of SCORTEN; event chains through fluid loss, infection, and AKI carry most downstream risk.
Sepsis is a major mortality pathway in SJS/TEN.
AKI and elevated BUN reflect poor reserve and multiorgan failure.
Respiratory failure, airway sloughing, pneumonia, and ARDS worsen short-term survival.
Hypoperfusion and volume loss increase AKI risk.
Fever and CRP share systemic inflammatory and infection drivers.
Skin and mucosal epithelial necrolysis are both driven by cytotoxic epithelial injury.
SCORTEN is an externally observed prognostic composite; use carefully to avoid double-counting when all components are already present.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stopping the true culprit removes antigenic drive.
If all likely culprits are already withdrawn, the remaining action is documentation and avoidance.

failure_modes: new high-risk drug added during admission
treatments.context_specific_role: Core trigger-removal intervention when a plausible culprit exposure exists.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large detached BSA needs thermoregulation, non-adherent dressings, infection control, analgesia, and nutrition.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive care analogous to burn care but with SJS/TEN-specific mucosal and ocular protection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large barrier loss requires early volume, electrolyte, protein, temperature, and caloric support.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema or ARDS risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Organ-support backbone for large BSA detachment, poor oral intake, AKI risk, and catabolic state.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Early ocular surface treatment prevents symblepharon and corneal scarring.

failure_modes: amniotic membrane delayed in severe epithelial loss
treatments.context_specific_role: Dedicated ocular pathway for any acute eye involvement; systemic skin improvement alone does not protect the ocular surface.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active sepsis reduces the benefit-to-risk ratio and increases infection complications.
Immunomodulation is more plausible during active progression than after re-epithelialization.

side_effects.interpretation: Immunosuppression increases infection risk, especially with open skin or sepsis.

failure_modes: late start after progression has stopped
treatments.context_specific_role: Immunomodulatory option during active progression; risk-benefit depends on infection, diabetes, and timing.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Nephrotoxicity limits cyclosporine use in AKI or advanced CKD.

treatments.context_specific_role: T-cell targeted systemic immunomodulation for active epidermal necrolysis when renal and infection context allows.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Often used in severe progressive SJS/TEN, though efficacy estimates vary.
IVIG can worsen renal function depending on formulation and volume load.

side_effects.interpretation: AKI risk from IVIG formulation, volume, or thrombosis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct systemic immunomodulation in severe active disease; not a substitute for trigger withdrawal and supportive care.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TNF blockade increases concern for active infection and reactivation.

side_effects.interpretation: TNF blockade can increase infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Targeted cytokine immunomodulation used in some severe progressive cases.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Extracorporeal therapy may worsen hemodynamic instability.

failure_modes: insufficient effect on ongoing antigen exposure
treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue adjunct for selected severe progressive cases or when mediator/drug removal is being attempted.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antimicrobials treat true wound infection, bacteremia, pneumonia, or sepsis.
Unnecessary high-risk antibiotics can confuse culprit attribution or worsen SCAR risk.

side_effects.interpretation: New high-risk antimicrobial exposure may become a competing culprit context.

failure_modes: fungal infection not covered when present
treatments.context_specific_role: Treats documented or strongly suspected infection; should be guided by cultures and allergy/culprit review.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Airway epithelial injury can deteriorate quickly and requires gentle airway planning.

side_effects.interpretation: Ventilator-associated pneumonia and airway trauma risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Life-support intervention for airway, hypoxemia, or ARDS complications.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RRT is relevant when AKI produces severe uremia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, or fluid overload.

side_effects.interpretation: Hemodynamic intolerance, especially with intermittent dialysis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Organ support for severe AKI or electrolyte/acid-base complications.

supportive_care: Stop all suspected culprit and cross-reactive drugs immediately; document the culprit probability and drug-avoidance list in the medical record.
Admit extensive or rapidly progressive disease to a dermatology, ICU, or burn-capable unit with non-adherent wound care, temperature regulation, analgesia, nutrition, and infection surveillance.
Estimate and trend detached BSA and total involved BSA daily; calculate SCORTEN when components are available, but avoid double-counting when individual components are already entered.

Daily or more frequent monitoring during active disease: vital signs, fluid balance, urine output, CBC with differential, electrolytes, bicarbonate, BUN/creatinine, glucose, albumin, AST/ALT, cultures if infection suspected, and pain control needs.
Avoid adhesive trauma; use non-adherent dressings, sterile handling, gentle debridement only when indicated, and pressure-injury prevention.

Early ophthalmology examination for any eye symptom or facial/mucosal involvement; use preservative-free lubrication, topical anti-inflammatory/antibiotic strategy as appropriate, symblepharon prevention, and amniotic membrane transplantation for severe ocular epithelial defects.
Oral, genital, and urinary mucosal care: pain control, bland rinses, barrier protection, catheter avoidance when possible, and gynecology/urology input for severe genital involvement.
Provide enteral or parenteral nutrition when oral intake is limited by mucositis, odynophagia, or GI involvement.
Use antimicrobials for documented or strongly suspected infection or sepsis; choose agents with attention to the suspected culprit list and culture data.

Screen for airway involvement when hoarseness, dyspnea, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, extensive oral sloughing, or progressive respiratory symptoms occur; plan gentle airway support if deterioration is likely.

Consider systemic immunomodulation based on active progression, infection status, renal function, timing, and local expertise; do not let immunomodulation replace trigger withdrawal and supportive care.
After discharge, follow for ocular sequelae, genital adhesions, pigment change, nail loss, dry eye, visual loss, post-ICU weakness, psychological sequelae, and lifelong drug avoidance.
